lead: A cockpit is a human-machine interface (HMI): the place where a crew senses aircraft state, decides, and acts. It exists because displays, controls and warnings must match human limits of attention, memory and reaction time. Good design makes the normal flow smooth and the abnormal case obvious. It is used in every aircraft, from a two-seat trainer to a long-haul jet. Only a few universities teach this topic in depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.4 for display formats and Chapter 4.5 for eyes-out displays.

sections.h3: The cockpit as a human-machine interface

blocks.text: The crew works in a loop: sense, decide, act. The HMI supplies the sense and act parts. Displays show state. Controls change state. Warnings interrupt when state is unsafe. Automation carries long tasks. The pilot stays at the top because the crew remains responsible.

Information hierarchy means importance decides position. Primary flight data — attitude, airspeed, altitude, heading — sits in the forward view. Navigation and systems data sit on multi-function displays (MFDs) and need a deliberate look. Menus hold less urgent data. The more often a value is used and the less time the crew has to react, the nearer it must be to the eyes.

Controls follow the same logic. Frequent controls sit on the stick or throttle, or near the pilot's hand. Infrequent controls sit on panels. Every control must show its effect: a switch position, a light, or a display echo.

Colour carries meaning only if used consistently. Common civil convention: red for warning, amber for caution, green for normal, white for advisory, magenta for the active route. Colour must never be the only cue. A shape, text or sound must repeat it, because colour vision varies and sunlight washes out screens.

Alerts come in levels. A warning needs immediate action (fire, stall). A caution needs timely attention (low fuel, system fault). An advisory is information (a mode change). Master warning and master caution lights gather the first alert so the crew looks at the right system page. Aural alerts use different tones; the sound must stand out from cockpit noise.

Usability rules of the FAR/CS 25.1302 kind ask that a crew can detect, understand and respond to every alert, without hazard from the design itself. The alert must say what is wrong and what action is required. A master caution that flashes for every trivial fault trains the crew to ignore it.

sections.h3: Controls, workload and automation mode awareness

blocks.text: Workload is not constant. Take-off and landing are high-workload; cruise is low. The HMI must reduce peak workload and keep the crew monitoring in low workload. Error and fatigue make this harder: people skip checks, misread similar values, and trust a silent automation. Design uses checklists, standard callouts, and clear failure messages.

Automation mode awareness means the crew always knows what the automation is doing and what it will do next. The flight mode annunciator (FMA) shows active and armed modes. A silent mode change is a design fault. Mode confusion — the crew thinks the aircraft is in one mode but it is in another — is a known accident factor.

items: Is the most urgent information nearest the eyes?
Does every alert name the fault and the action?
Is colour backed by text or shape?
Is the automation mode always visible?
Can the crew recover from a mistake without a hidden mode?

figure.caption: The crew sits at the top of the HMI stack; displays and warnings carry information, controls carry action, and automation sits below as a system the crew supervises.

spec.aria: A five-layer stack from pilot at top through displays, controls and warnings to automation at bottom, with crew above and systems below.

examples.question: A pilot scans 6 displays with 0.4 s dwell per display. Find one full scan time. If a warning must be seen within 2 s, is one full scan enough?
steps: Scan time = number of displays × dwell per display = 6 × 0.4 s = 2.4 s.
Compare: 2.4 s > 2 s, so one full scan is not enough.
Therefore the warning needs a separate salient channel: master warning light and aural alert.
examples.answer: One full scan takes 2.4 s; it is not enough for a 2 s warning budget, so the warning must be separate and salient.
examples.check:
dwell = 0.4
displays = 6
scan = displays * dwell
budget = 2.0
print(scan)
print(budget)

traps: More information on screen is not better HMI; clutter raises scan time and hides faults.
Red, amber and green are not decoration; using red for normal values destroys warning meaning.
A master caution for every minor fault causes alarm fatigue; crews ignore real alerts.
Mode confusion is not only pilot error; a silent or hidden mode change is a design failure.

quiz.a: The interface between crew and aircraft systems through displays, controls and warnings.

quiz.q: Name the three alert levels and give an example of each.
quiz.a: Warning: fire. Caution: low fuel. Advisory: mode change.

quiz.q: Why must colour never be the only cue?
quiz.a: Colour vision varies, sunlight washes out screens, and monochrome backup must work; add text, shape or sound.

quiz.q: A crew scans 5 displays at 0.5 s each. Find scan time. Is one scan within a 2 s caution budget?
A new engine page adds 40 parameters. Give two HMI risks and one fix.
quiz.a: Clutter raises scan time and hides abnormal values; fix with hierarchy, declutter, or alert-driven pages.

quiz.q: Explain mode confusion and give one design fix.
quiz.a: Crew believes automation is in mode A but it is in B; fix with a clear FMA, mode-change alert, and visible armed modes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry work uses human factors standards, simulator trials and eye-tracking to measure scan patterns. Newer cockpits add touchscreens, head-up guidance and voice alerting, so the same questions return: what is the crew's attention budget, and what happens when automation is silent? Search for human factors, crew resource management, mode awareness and alert fatigue. Read accident reports for HMI lessons.
